body_markdown:
Though Toyota makes a lovely little sports car, when it comes to full-size SUVs the Japanese brand wholeheartedly embraces the “bigger is better” philosophy that resonates so well with American consumers. We also love being adventure-ready at any time, so it is no surprise that Toyota’s overlanding-focused package, Trailhunter, is coming to the brand’s body-on-frame SUV for 2027. We’ve been[anticipating the Sequoia Trailhunter](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/toyota-adds-trailhunter-packages-to-2027-tundra-and-sequoia/) for a while now, and at the Specialty Equipment Market Association show (SEMA), Toyota dished some more details.


Toyota | Benjamin Hutton


Toyota | Benjamin Hutton


Toyota | Benjamin Hutton


Toyota | Benjamin Hutton


The 2027 Toyota Sequoia Trailhunter will be based on the entry-level trim (SR5). Perhaps for that reason, the SR5 no longer gets a smaller (8-inch) infotainment screen than the other models. All receive the big 14-incher and, for 2027, the Drive Recorder Dash Cam that recruits the suite of exterior cameras to capture 20-second clips either automatically or on-demand. As before, all Trailhunters use the i-Force Max hybrid powertrain: a 3.4-liter twin-turbo V-6 “with a specially designed motor generator” that delivers 437 net combined hp and 583 lb-ft of torque (the same figures as 2026). Towing capacity carries over as well, at 9520 pounds.


Toyota | Benjamin Hutton


The Trailhunter is differentiated from the TRD Pro in that the former is a package on the SR5, the latter is its own trim. We are eager to hear more about the philosophy behind each off-road-oriented configuration, and the suspension options begin to sketch out the picture: The TRD Pro, described as “the ultimate off-road SUV by Toyota,” upgrades from 2.5-inch Fox Internal Bypass coilovers and remote reservoir rear shocks to Fox’s venerable QS3 shocks. Currently offered for motorcycles and snowmobiles, these offer three different settings (soft, medium, and firm) that are easily adjustable without any tools.


Toyota | Benjamin Hutton


Toyota | Benjamin Hutton


Toyota | Benjamin Hutton


The Trailhunter package brings 2.5-inch forged monotube position-sensitive shocks with rear piggyback reservoirs made not by Fox but by Old Man Emu. From what we know, the Sequoia Trailhunter’s setup won’t be adjustable like the TRD Pro version’s. Leaving the fancier shocks to the (likely far more expensive) TRD Pro makes sense, since according to the blueprint laid by the Tacoma, the two configurations have[different price points and different focuses](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-drive-2024-toyota-tacoma-hybrid-is-a-radical-leap-forward-and-a-spendy-one/) : The overlanding-focused Trailhunter will see most of its off-roading at slow speeds with relatively high payload in the form of camping apparatus, and the desert-running TRD Pro will have the adjustability it needs to run across different terrain at higher speeds.


We don’t know pricing yet, except for the base model. The figure is significantly higher, as you might expect with all the updates plus the reality of inflation: $72,095 versus $67,920.


Stay tuned for more information on this big, off-road brute: We’re heading to Texas next week to drive the 2027 Sequoia and talk to the people who made it. If you have questions you’d like answered, drop them in the comments below!


Toyota | Benjamin Hutton
